q: In a classroom demonstration, a chicken bone is soaked in vinegar until its mineral salts dissolve. The bone keeps its shape but can now be bent easily. Which matrix component remains and gives this flexibility?
w: Bone matrix is about one-third organic, mostly collagen (flexibility and tensile strength), and two-thirds inorganic calcium phosphate as hydroxyapatite (hardness). Acid dissolves the mineral and leaves the collagen framework, so the bone bends.

n.1: Osteocytes maintain the matrix but are cells, not the fibrous part of the matrix that resists bending forces.
n.2: Elastin gives stretch and recoil in skin and elastic cartilage; the organic fiber of bone matrix is collagen.
n.3: Hydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness and is the part the acid dissolves; once it is gone the bone loses rigidity.

q: A 64-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis several years after menopause. Which change in bone remodeling best accounts for her loss of bone mass?
o: Calcitonin rises and stimulates osteoclast resorption
Osteoblasts resorb more matrix as estrogen declines
w: Bone is constantly remodeled by osteoblasts (which build) and osteoclasts (which resorb). After menopause estrogen falls, resorption exceeds formation, and bone mass is lost: osteoporosis.

n.0: If formation outpaced resorption, bone mass would increase rather than decrease.
n.2: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; it does not stimulate bone resorption.
n.3: Osteoblasts build bone; resorbing matrix is the job of osteoclasts.

q: Blood calcium drops below its normal range, and the parathyroid glands respond by increasing hormone secretion. What effect does this hormone have on bone tissue?
o: Osteoblast activity rises, depositing Ca²⁺ into the matrix
Osteoclast activity rises, releasing Ca²⁺ from the matrix
Osteoclast activity falls, keeping Ca²⁺ stored in the matrix
Calcitonin release rises, moving Ca²⁺ out of the matrix
w: Step 1: low blood Ca²⁺ triggers release of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Step 2: PTH raises blood Ca²⁺ by stimulating osteoclast activity, which resorbs matrix and releases Ca²⁺ (bone stores about 99% of the body's calcium).

n.0: Osteoblast deposition would move calcium out of the blood and into bone, the opposite of what PTH achieves.
n.2: Reducing osteoclast activity lowers blood Ca²⁺, which matches calcitonin, not PTH.
n.3: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid gland, not the parathyroids, and it lowers blood calcium rather than releasing it from bone.

q: During fetal development, most bones form by replacing a hyaline cartilage model. Which bone instead forms directly within a fibrous membrane by intramembranous ossification?
w: Intramembranous ossification builds bone directly in a fibrous membrane: the flat bones of the skull, the clavicles and some facial bones. Long bones and vertebrae form by endochondral ossification, replacing a hyaline cartilage model.

n.0: The humerus is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.
n.1: Vertebrae are irregular bones that form by endochondral ossification from cartilage models.
n.2: The femur is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.

q: A surgeon reattaches a torn tendon to the outer surface of a long bone. Which structure covers that surface, carries blood vessels and nerves, and adds bone to increase the bone's width?
w: The periosteum is the outer membrane of a bone: it carries vessels and nerves, anchors tendons, and adds bone to the surface (appositional growth in width) and during repair.

n.0: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces, is avascular and does not anchor tendons or add width.
n.1: The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavity, not the outer surface where tendons attach.
n.3: The synovial membrane lines a joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid; tendons do not anchor to it.

q: After six months on a space station, an astronaut has lost bone density in the legs despite eating a normal diet. Which principle best explains this loss?
o: Bone remodels in response to the mechanical stress on it
Osteoclasts resorb bone when blood calcium rises above normal
Bone mass is fixed once the epiphyseal plates close
Calcitonin rises when the skeleton bears less weight
w: Bone remodeling responds to mechanical stress (Wolff's law): weight-bearing load stimulates bone formation. Without load, resorption by osteoclasts exceeds formation by osteoblasts, so bone density falls.

n.1: High blood calcium triggers calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts; resorption is driven by low blood calcium (PTH) and, in this case, by the loss of mechanical load.
n.2: Bone is remodeled throughout life; adults gain or lose bone mass long after the growth plates close.
n.3: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, so it would tend to preserve bone; it does not explain the loss.

q: A student is sorting bones into the axial and appendicular divisions of the skeleton. Which of the following bones belongs to the axial skeleton?
w: The axial skeleton (80 bones) is the skull, hyoid, auditory ossicles, vertebral column and rib cage. The pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula) and the pelvic girdle (hip bones) belong to the appendicular skeleton.

n.0: The hip bones form the pelvic girdle, which is appendicular even though it joins the sacrum.
n.1: The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.
n.3: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.

q: A physical therapist moves a patient's thigh through flexion, abduction, rotation and circumduction at the hip, then bends and straightens the elbow at the humeroulnar joint. Which pairing correctly classifies these two synovial joints?
w: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded femoral head sits in the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing multiaxial movement including rotation and circumduction. The humeroulnar joint is a uniaxial hinge that allows flexion and extension; forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints, the proximal one being a pivot.

n.0: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge that allows only flexion and extension; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint, which rotates the radius.
n.2: The hip is not condyloid: condyloid (ellipsoid) joints such as the wrist are biaxial and do not allow true rotation, which the hip performs.
n.3: Both are misclassified: a condyloid joint cannot rotate as the hip does, and the humeroulnar joint is a hinge, not the radioulnar pivot.

q: Which set gives the correct number of separate vertebrae in each region of a typical adult's vertebral column, listed as cervical, thoracic, lumbar?
w: An adult has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic (one for each pair of ribs) and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx: 26 bones in all.

n.0: This swaps the cervical and lumbar counts; the neck has 7 cervical vertebrae.
n.1: This swaps the cervical and thoracic counts; there are 12 thoracic vertebrae to match the 12 pairs of ribs.
n.2: This swaps the thoracic and lumbar counts; there are 5 large lumbar vertebrae.

q: Which ribs are called floating ribs because they have no anterior attachment to the sternum, either directly or through costal cartilage?
w: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum. Ribs 8 to 12 are false ribs: 8 to 10 attach through the cartilage of rib 7, and 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no anterior attachment.

n.0: Ribs 8 to 12 are the false ribs; within that group, 8 to 10 still attach indirectly, so they do not float.
n.2: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs that attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage.
n.3: Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs that reach the sternum indirectly through rib 7's costal cartilage.

q: In anatomical position, which pairing correctly describes where the radius lies in the forearm and where the tibia lies in the leg?
w: In anatomical position (palms forward) the radius is on the lateral, thumb side of the forearm and the ulna is medial. In the leg the large, weight-bearing tibia is medial and the thin fibula is lateral.

n.0: The tibia is medial; the lateral leg bone is the fibula.
n.2: The radius is lateral; the medial forearm bone is the ulna.
n.3: Both are reversed: the ulna is the medial forearm bone and the fibula is the lateral leg bone.

q: How are the sutures that join the cranial bones of an adult skull classified, both by structure and by the amount of movement they allow?
o: Cartilaginous joints that are slightly movable
Fibrous joints that are slightly movable
w: Sutures are fibrous joints: the bones are held together by short connective tissue fibers with no joint cavity. Functionally they are synarthroses (immovable).

n.0: Slightly movable cartilaginous joints (symphyses) include the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs.
n.1: Immovable cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) include the epiphyseal plate and the first rib-sternum joint, not sutures.
n.2: A slightly movable fibrous joint is a syndesmosis, such as the distal tibiofibular joint; sutures are immovable.

q: Which type of tissue forms the intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee, where it resists compression and absorbs shock between bones?
w: Fibrocartilage is the strongest, most shock-absorbing cartilage, with thick collagen bundles. It forms the intervertebral discs, the knee menisci and the pubic symphysis.

n.0: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces and forms costal cartilage and growth plates; it is not the disc or meniscus tissue.
n.1: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, not the discs or menisci.
n.3: Elastic cartilage gives flexible support in the ear auricle and epiglottis.

q: Starting from anatomical position, a patient turns the forearm so that the palm faces backward, with the radius crossing over the ulna. What is this movement called?
w: Pronation turns the palm to face posteriorly (or downward) as the radius crosses over the ulna. Supination is the reverse, returning the palm to face anteriorly as in anatomical position.

n.0: Circumduction is a cone-shaped movement of a limb, as at the shoulder or hip.
n.1: Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward; it is a foot movement.
n.2: Supination turns the palm forward or upward; in anatomical position the forearm is already supinated.

q: Counting the carpals, metacarpals and phalanges, how many bones form the skeleton of one adult hand, from the wrist to the fingertips?
w: 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges = 27. The thumb has 2 phalanges and each of the other four fingers has 3, so the phalanges total 2 + (4 x 3) = 14.

n.0: This comes from giving the thumb 3 phalanges like the other fingers (8 + 5 + 15).
n.1: This comes from counting one phalanx per digit (8 + 5 + 5).
n.3: This comes from using 7 carpals, which is the number of tarsals in the foot (7 + 5 + 14).

q: In the classification of bones by shape, to which category does the patella (kneecap) belong?
w: Sesamoid bones form within tendons, and the patella is the classic example. Short bones are cube-like (carpals, tarsals), flat bones are thin (cranial bones, sternum, ribs, scapulae) and irregular bones include the vertebrae.

n.0: Irregular bones, such as the vertebrae, have complex shapes and do not develop within tendons.
n.1: Flat bones are thin and often curved, such as the cranial bones, sternum, ribs and scapulae.
n.3: Short bones are roughly cube-shaped, such as the carpals and tarsals, and do not form inside tendons.

q: A tissue sample shows branched, striated cells, each with one central nucleus, joined end to end by intercalated discs. From which location was the sample most likely taken?
w: Branched, striated cells with usually one nucleus, joined by intercalated discs (gap junctions plus desmosomes), are cardiac muscle, found only in the heart wall.

n.0: The stomach wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells without intercalated discs.
n.1: Artery walls contain smooth muscle, which is nonstriated and lacks intercalated discs.
n.2: The biceps brachii is skeletal muscle: long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers without intercalated discs.

q: A histology lab compares the three muscle types. Which description matches smooth muscle, such as the muscle found in the wall of the small intestine?
o: Spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus, nonstriated, involuntary
Branched cells, intercalated discs, striated, involuntary
Long cylindrical cells, many nuclei, striated, voluntary
Spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus, striated, involuntary
w: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (fusiform) with one nucleus, lack striations and are under involuntary control by the autonomic nervous system and hormones. They produce slow, sustained contractions such as peristalsis.

n.1: Branched, striated, involuntary cells joined by intercalated discs describe cardiac muscle.
n.2: Long, cylindrical, multinucleated, striated, voluntary fibers describe skeletal muscle.
n.3: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, single-nucleated and involuntary, but they lack striations; striation marks skeletal and cardiac muscle.

q: When the right and left sternocleidomastoid muscles contract together, what movement results?
o: Elevate the mandible to close the jaw
Extend the head and lift the chin
Flex the head toward the chest
Elevate the shoulders toward the ears
w: Each sternocleidomastoid runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. Acting together, the two flex the head and neck toward the chest; one acting alone rotates the head toward the opposite side.

n.0: Closing the jaw is the action of the masseter, which elevates the mandible.
n.1: Extending the head is an action of posterior muscles such as the trapezius, the opposite of what the sternocleidomastoids do together.
n.3: Elevating the shoulders (shrugging) is the action of the trapezius.

q: A person lifts a grocery bag by flexing the elbow. Which muscle acts as the antagonist to the prime mover during this movement?
w: In elbow flexion the biceps brachii is the agonist (prime mover). The triceps brachii, which extends the elbow, is the antagonist: it relaxes and stretches as the biceps contracts.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.
n.1: The biceps brachii is the prime mover (agonist) of elbow flexion, not its antagonist.
n.2: The deltoid abducts the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.

q: During elbow flexion, the biceps brachii pulls the radius toward the shoulder while its attachments on the scapula stay fixed. How is the attachment on the radius classified?
o: Origin, because it is on the bone that moves
Origin, because it is farther from the trunk
Insertion, because it is on the bone that moves
Insertion, because it is on the stationary bone
w: The origin is the attachment on the more stationary bone (here the scapula); the insertion is on the bone that moves (the radius). During contraction the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

n.0: The attachment on the moving bone is the insertion; the origin is on the more stationary bone.
n.1: Origin and insertion are defined by which bone moves, not by distance from the trunk; the moving radius carries the insertion.
n.3: The insertion is on the bone that moves; the stationary attachment is the origin.

q: Standing in a cold wind, a hiker begins to shiver. Which statement best explains how shivering helps maintain body temperature?
o: Dermal blood vessels dilate, carrying warm blood out to the skin
Cardiac muscle beats faster, and its extra contractions make the heat
Smooth muscle in vessel walls contracts rhythmically and releases heat
Skeletal muscles contract involuntarily, releasing heat as they use ATP
w: Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscle triggered by the hypothalamus. Much of the energy released as the muscles use ATP is lost as heat, so heat production rises and body temperature is maintained. Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat but does not produce it.

n.0: Dilation of dermal vessels sends warm blood to the surface and releases heat; in the cold these vessels constrict to conserve it.
n.1: A faster heartbeat is not shivering; shivering is repeated contraction of the large mass of skeletal muscle, which is the main source of the extra heat.
n.2: Shivering is contraction of skeletal muscle, not vascular smooth muscle; narrowing of dermal vessels conserves heat but is not shivering.

q: A patient is asked to rise up onto the toes. Which movement occurs at the ankle, and which muscles act as the prime movers?
o: Plantar flexion by the tibialis anterior
Dorsiflexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
Plantar flexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
w: Step 1: rising onto the toes points the foot downward, which is plantar flexion. Step 2: the prime movers of plantar flexion are the gastrocnemius and soleus, acting through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

n.0: The tibialis anterior produces dorsiflexion, not plantar flexion.
n.1: The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the ankle; dorsiflexion is the action of the tibialis anterior.
n.2: Dorsiflexion lifts the toes toward the shin, the opposite of rising onto the toes.

q: Climbing a steep flight of stairs needs strong extension at the hip. Which muscle is the prime mover of hip extension and the largest muscle of the buttock?
w: The gluteus maximus, the largest muscle of the buttock, is the prime mover of hip extension, as in climbing stairs or rising from a chair. The hamstrings assist it.

n.0: The iliopsoas flexes the hip, the opposite movement.
n.1: The rectus femoris, one of the quadriceps, flexes the hip and extends the knee.
n.3: The gluteus medius lies deeper and higher on the hip; it abducts the hip and steadies the pelvis during walking.

q: A nurse asks a patient to raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder. Which muscle is the prime mover for this abduction of the arm?
w: The deltoid, which caps the shoulder, is the prime mover of arm abduction (moving the arm away from the midline). It is also a common intramuscular injection site.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
n.1: The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, the opposite direction to abduction.
n.2: The trapezius elevates and retracts the scapula and extends the head; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder joint.

q: During quiet, restful breathing, which muscles contract to enlarge the thoracic cavity so that air flows into the lungs?
w: In quiet inspiration the diaphragm (the main muscle of inspiration) contracts and flattens while the external intercostals lift the ribs. Both enlarge the thoracic cavity, pressure in the lungs falls and air flows in. Quiet expiration is mostly passive recoil; the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles act in forced expiration.

n.0: The external intercostals do help, but the rectus abdominis flexes the trunk and assists forced expiration, and the diaphragm is missing.
n.1: The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles such as the rectus abdominis are muscles of forced expiration, not inspiration.
n.3: The diaphragm is right, but the internal intercostals pull the ribs down during forced expiration; they do not act in quiet inspiration.

q: Which of the following structures is made of smooth muscle?
w: The arrector pili are small bundles of smooth muscle attached to hair follicles; their contraction makes hairs stand up (goosebumps). Other smooth muscle sites include blood vessels, airways, the iris and hollow organs.

n.0: The myocardium is cardiac muscle: involuntary like smooth muscle, but striated, with branched cells joined by intercalated discs.
n.2: Muscles of facial expression are striated, voluntary skeletal muscles, even though many insert into the skin rather than onto bone.
n.3: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle; it contracts automatically during quiet breathing but is striated and can be controlled voluntarily.

q: When a skeletal muscle fiber is stimulated, calcium ions flood the sarcoplasm. To which protein do these calcium ions bind directly to begin the process of contraction?
w: Ca²⁺ binds troponin on the thin filament. This shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can form cross-bridges.

n.0: Tropomyosin is the strand that covers actin's binding sites; it is moved by troponin, not bound by Ca²⁺.
n.2: Actin carries the binding sites for myosin; calcium acts on troponin, which then uncovers those sites.
n.3: Myosin heads bind actin and ATP; calcium does not bind myosin to start skeletal muscle contraction.

q: In a resting skeletal muscle fiber, most of the calcium that will trigger the next contraction is stored in which structure?
w: The sarcoplasmic reticulum, the muscle fiber's smooth ER, stores Ca²⁺ and releases it when an action potential arrives; during relaxation the Ca²⁺ is pumped back in using ATP.

n.0: The sarcolemma is the muscle cell membrane that conducts the action potential; it is not the internal calcium store.
n.2: T-tubules carry the action potential deep into the fiber; they do not store the calcium.
n.3: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration; they are not the calcium store that triggers contraction.

q: A toxin blocks acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Which effect on the skeletal muscle fiber is expected?
o: ACh stays in the cleft and keeps stimulating the fiber
ACh release stops, so the fiber cannot be stimulated
Myosin heads cannot detach, as in rigor mortis
Ca²⁺ cannot leave the sarcoplasmic reticulum
w: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft so the fiber can relax. If the enzyme is blocked, ACh lingers and keeps binding its receptors, so the fiber is stimulated again and again.

n.1: The enzyme breaks ACh down after release; blocking it does not stop the motor neuron from releasing ACh.
n.2: Myosin fails to detach when ATP runs out, as after death; this toxin affects ACh breakdown, not ATP supply.
n.3: Calcium release follows the muscle action potential, which lingering ACh makes more likely, not less.

q: During a strong concentric contraction of the biceps brachii, which change occurs within each sarcomere of its fibers?
o: The H zone widens as the Z discs move apart
The A band shortens while the I band keeps its length
The I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length
The actin and myosin filaments shorten as the Z discs move closer
w: In the sliding filament model, thin actin filaments slide toward the M line: the Z discs move closer and the I band and H zone shorten. The A band equals the length of the thick myosin filaments, so it stays the same. The filaments slide; they do not shorten.

n.0: In contraction the H zone narrows and the Z discs move closer together, not apart.
n.1: The A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten; it is the I band that narrows.
n.3: Neither filament shortens; actin and myosin slide past each other while keeping their lengths.

q: A few hours after death, the skeletal muscles of the body become stiff and rigid. Which explanation of this rigor mortis is correct?
o: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Excess acetylcholine keeps restimulating the fibers
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot attach to actin
Without calcium, troponin keeps tropomyosin in place
w: Step 1: after death, ATP production stops. Step 2: ATP must bind a myosin head to release it from actin, so the cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles remain rigid.

n.1: Acetylcholine release requires living motor neurons and is cleared by acetylcholinesterase; the stiffness comes from the lack of ATP.
n.2: If myosin could not attach, the muscles would stay limp; the problem is that attached heads cannot let go.
n.3: Tropomyosin blocking actin would prevent cross-bridges and keep muscle relaxed, not rigid.

q: The same arm muscles are used to lift a pencil and then a heavy suitcase. How does the nervous system chiefly increase the force the muscle produces for the suitcase?
o: Each fiber contracts harder in response to a single impulse
More motor units are recruited to contract at once
The myosin filaments lengthen to form more cross-bridges
More troponin is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
w: A single fiber follows the all-or-none principle, so whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units (one motor neuron plus all the fibers it supplies) and by raising the frequency of stimulation.

n.0: Each fiber responds all-or-none to an impulse; force is graded at the level of the whole muscle.
n.2: Myofilaments keep their length during contraction; they slide past one another.
n.3: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺, not troponin; troponin is part of the thin filament.

q: During a 10-second sprint, a runner quickly uses up the ATP already stored in the leg muscles. Which source then regenerates ATP most rapidly for the next several seconds?
w: Muscle energy sources come into play in sequence: stored ATP (a few seconds), then creatine phosphate, which transfers its phosphate to ADP almost instantly (about 10 to 15 seconds), then anaerobic glycolysis, then aerobic respiration.

n.0: Myoglobin stores oxygen for aerobic respiration; it does not regenerate ATP directly.
n.1: Aerobic respiration yields the most ATP but is the slowest pathway, so it is not the most rapid source.
n.3: Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but follows creatine phosphate as the main source after the first several seconds.

q: During an all-out 400-meter sprint, lactic acid builds up in a runner's leg muscles. Which process produces this lactic acid?
o: Glycolysis when oxygen supply is short
Hydrolysis of ATP by myosin heads
w: When oxygen delivery cannot meet demand, pyruvate from glycolysis is converted to lactic acid. Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but yields 2 ATP per glucose.

n.0: Creatine phosphate donates its phosphate to ADP, leaving creatine; it does not form lactic acid.
n.2: Myosin's hydrolysis of ATP yields ADP and phosphate to power the stroke; it does not form lactic acid.
n.3: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, not lactic acid.

q: Skeletal muscle fibers are wide cells, yet all their myofibrils contract almost at the same moment. What do the transverse (T) tubules do that makes this possible?
o: Carry the impulse deep into the fiber
Anchor thin filaments at each Z disc
w: T-tubules are inward folds of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fiber, next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so Ca²⁺ is released around every myofibril at once.

n.0: Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in the T-tubules.
n.1: Acetylcholine is released by the motor neuron's axon terminal at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Thin filaments are anchored at the Z discs themselves; T-tubules conduct the impulse.

q: A patient slowly lowers a dumbbell from shoulder height to the thigh, keeping the elbow under control. What type of contraction is the biceps brachii performing?
w: Isotonic contractions change muscle length: concentric contractions shorten the muscle (curling the weight up) and eccentric contractions lengthen it while it stays under tension (lowering the weight slowly). Isometric contractions build tension with no change in length.

n.0: The biceps is not relaxed here: it stays under tension to control the descent, or the weight would simply drop.
n.1: A concentric contraction shortens the muscle, as when the dumbbell is curled up toward the shoulder.
n.3: An isometric contraction builds tension with no change in length, as when the dumbbell is held still.

q: A new keratinocyte formed in the stratum basale is pushed toward the skin surface. Which epidermal layer does it enter next?
w: Epidermal layers from deep to superficial: stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (thick skin only) and corneum. A cell leaving the basale enters the stratum spinosum first.

n.0: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer of dead cells, the last layer the cell reaches.
n.2: The stratum lucidum is present only in thick skin and lies just below the corneum, far from the basale.
n.3: The stratum granulosum lies above the spinosum, so the cell reaches it later.

q: A patient's skin and the whites of the eyes both look yellow. Buildup of which pigment best explains this color change?
w: Jaundice is a yellow color of the skin and the sclerae caused by bilirubin, a pigment formed when hemoglobin is broken down. Carotene can tint skin yellow-orange but does not yellow the sclerae.

n.0: Melanin is the brown-black pigment from melanocytes; more of it darkens the skin rather than turning it yellow.
n.1: Oxygenated hemoglobin gives skin a pink tone; too little oxygen causes a bluish color (cyanosis), not yellowing.
n.3: Carotene from orange and yellow vegetables can tint the skin yellow-orange, but it does not turn the whites of the eyes yellow.

q: A tissue sample taken just beneath the epidermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and a dense mesh of collagen and elastin fibers. Which layer and tissue type does it show?
o: Smooth muscle tissue of the dermis
w: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is connective tissue: areolar in the papillary layer and dense irregular in the reticular layer, rich in collagen (strength) and elastin (stretch), with vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

n.0: The dermis does contain tiny arrector pili muscles, but its main tissue is connective tissue, not smooth muscle.
n.2: The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; it has no blood vessels or collagen mesh.
n.3: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat with areolar tissue, not a dense collagen and elastin mesh.

q: Which sweat glands are distributed over most of the body surface, open directly onto the skin through pores, and secrete watery sweat that cools the body?
w: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands are the most numerous, are found almost everywhere (especially palms, soles and forehead), open onto the surface through pores and secrete watery sweat for thermoregulation.

n.0: Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, usually into hair follicles; they do not produce sweat.
n.2: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands in the ear canal that produce earwax.
n.3: Apocrine glands are found in the axillary and anogenital regions, open into hair follicles and become active at puberty.

q: A biopsy from the sole of the foot shows a clear layer of flattened dead cells between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum. A biopsy from the upper arm lacks it. Which layer is this?
w: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear layer between the granulosum and corneum that is present in the thick skin of the palms and soles and absent from thin skin.

n.0: The papillary layer is the superficial part of the dermis, below the whole epidermis.
n.1: The stratum spinosum lies below the granulosum and is present in both thick and thin skin.
n.2: The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer and is present in all skin.

q: A patient who spends almost no time outdoors develops low blood calcium. Which sequence best describes the skin's normal role in calcium absorption from the intestine?
o: Melanocytes secrete vitamin D3 after UVB exposure; the kidneys then activate it
UVB converts a cholesterol derivative directly into active calcitriol in skin
Sebaceous glands secrete vitamin D3 in sebum; the liver then activates it
UVB makes vitamin D3 from a cholesterol derivative; liver and kidneys activate it
w: Step 1: in the skin, UVB converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D3, an inactive precursor. Step 2: the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol, which increases calcium absorption from the gut. Little sun means little D3 and poorer Ca²⁺ absorption.

n.0: Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative in the skin, and the liver also takes part in activation.
n.1: The skin makes only the precursor; activation to calcitriol takes place in the liver and kidneys.
n.2: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum to lubricate skin; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative, and the kidneys also take part in activation.

q: While jogging on a hot afternoon, a person's body temperature starts to rise. Which pair of skin responses is mainly responsible for releasing the excess heat?
o: Dermal vessels constrict; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels constrict; arrector pili muscles contract
Dermal vessels dilate; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels dilate; apocrine glands secrete sweat
w: To lose heat, dermal blood vessels dilate so more warm blood reaches the surface, and eccrine glands secrete watery sweat that cools the skin as it evaporates.

n.0: Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat, the opposite of what is needed here.
n.1: Vessel constriction and arrector pili contraction are heat-conserving responses to cold.
n.3: Apocrine glands in the axillae and groin respond mainly to stress and puberty; eccrine glands are the main thermoregulators.

q: Which glands secrete an oily substance, usually into hair follicles, that softens skin and hair, slows water loss and helps inhibit bacterial growth?
w: Sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles. Sebum lubricates and softens skin and hair, slows water loss and is antibacterial. They are absent from the palms and soles.

n.1: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands that produce earwax in the ear canal.
n.2: Apocrine glands also open into hair follicles, but they secrete a thicker sweat, not oily sebum.
n.3: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface through pores and secrete watery sweat.

q: Two healthy adults have very different natural skin tones. Which difference between their skin best explains this?
o: The amount of melanin their melanocytes produce
The number of melanocytes in their stratum corneum
The number of melanocytes in their stratum basale
The amount of keratin made by their keratinocytes
w: People have similar numbers of melanocytes; differences in natural skin color come mainly from how much melanin those melanocytes produce (with smaller contributions from carotene and hemoglobin).

n.1: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale, not the dead stratum corneum.
n.2: Melanocyte numbers are similar between people; it is their melanin output that differs.
n.3: Keratin is a structural, waterproofing protein, not the main pigment behind skin tone.

q: Fingerprint ridges come from the dermal layer just beneath the epidermis, which also holds the receptors for light touch. Which layer is this?
w: The dermis has two layers. The thin, superficial papillary layer forms the dermal papillae that create fingerprint ridges and holds Meissner corpuscles for light touch. The deeper reticular layer is dense collagen and elastin with hair follicles, glands and Pacinian corpuscles.

n.1: The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis, not a layer of the dermis.
n.2: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat; it is not part of the dermis.
n.3: The reticular layer is the deeper, thicker part of the dermis; it does not form the ridges under the epidermis.
